title: TeraWulf Funds 760MW Gas Plant and Gives $100M in Utility Credits
summary:
The Muskie data center in Kentucky will double its contracted power capacity to 1 GW through a new agreement with Kentucky Power to accelerate AI infrastructure growth. To secure the energy, TeraWulf has agreed to pay the estimated financing costs for the utility's planned 760 MW combined cycle generation facility at Big Sandy and provide $100M in winter bill credits to residential customers over the first 10 years of the contract, per an 8-K filing and AEP release. These credits, starting in 2029, are expected to average $25 per month per household during the winter heating season.

The deal pulls the delivery of the second 500 MW phase forward to 2029 from 2030, while the first phase begins ramping in 2028. TeraWulf is currently evaluating further expansion to 2 GW and is upsizing its senior secured revolver from $250M to meet collateral requirements. Analysts estimate the 1 GW capacity could generate $2.4B in annual revenue once leased, while Kentucky Power plans to seek regulatory approvals from the Public Service Commission later this year.

selectedTweets.text:
Kentucky Power has recently been pushing a distinctly pro-data-center message. Its current data-center page says large-load customers can “help reduce how fast rates might otherwise increase” and “help fund a stronger, more reliable grid,” while emphasizing that data centers must provide financial guarantees and long-term payment commitments so existing customers aren’t stuck with stranded costs. 
Just Friday, Kentucky Power announced transmission upgrades for the Muskie Data Center Campus in Boyd County, explicitly framing them as supporting “continued economic development.”
There was also a pretty striking Kentucky Power quote earlier this year: the utility said it actively pursues economic development because it is “the best vehicle for eventually balancing or lowering electric rates.”

selectedTweets.text:
Interesting model here per the 8-K and $AEP release

>WULF agrees to pay estimated financing costs associated with construction of Kentucky Power's ($AEP) planned 760MWs combined cycle generation facility at Big Sandy.
>WULF offers to provide $100M in winter bill credits for Kentucky Power's residential customers over the first 10 years off the contract (estimates this will equate to ~$25 per month during winter heating season per customer, with credits beginning in 2029)
>Agreement includes collateral requirements from WULF (announced upsizing the senior secured revolver this morning, from current $250M)
>Kentucky Power will seek regulatory approvals later this year

"Paying the interest costs on 760MW of new gas generation". Here's how it likely works:

Kentucky Power is a regulated utility. It earns a regulator-approved return on plants once they're running, charged to customers through rates. While a plant is being built, the utility is borrowing and spending but collecting nothing. Normally it books those financing costs as AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction), adds them to the plant's price tag, and customers pay them later.

WULF appears to be covering that cost instead. The exact mechanics aren't disclosed yet: interest only or the utility's full return, paid as incurred or as a lump sum. Our guess, could be $100-300M over the build, depending on structure. AEP gets paid sooner, the plant goes into rates cheaper, and existing customers don't fund a plant built for a data center. Looks to be in line thematically with what the White House has demanded.

This is not behind-the-meter because WULF won't own the plant. It will pay tariff rates like any other customer, plus this carry. Expect it to pass through to the tenant in the lease. The Public Service Commission filing later this year will likely reveal more details.
